Summary

Executive Summary

The 4,355 jobs the shop released in 2025 earned 25.4% on $56.08M of revenue ("margin": price less the job's full manufacturing cost, as a share of price) against the 28.8% their estimates promised, and 7.4% of them lost money. Actual cost came in $852K over the jobs' estimates (96% of the cost measured): elements over estimate added $3.49M and elements under estimate took back $2.63M. The two largest elements are run hours ($1.70M over) and outside processing ($1.01M, of which $467K is ledger cost allocated to jobs and not an overrun on any estimate). What the job-level comparison showed, and the P&L could not, is that the overrun is broad and modest: the median job ran 1.08× its estimated run hours, the year's 25.4% was an average of jobs ranging from losses on 7.4% of them to margins above 39% on one job in ten, and the same part could do both in the same year. The table sets out what the shop can now see, the action each view supports, and what it comes to on the 2025 jobs. Nothing in it is projected forward.

Section 1

Job Margin Overview

The average 2025 job earned 21.2% margin against the 26.8% its estimate promised, and most jobs came in below their estimate. The P&L gave the shop one number: 25.4% on $56.08M of revenue. The job record shows what that number averaged over: 2,586 jobs (59%) at or above the 21.9% the standard markup gives, 1,447 (33%) below it, and 322 (7.4%) that lost money, 2.9% of revenue because the losing jobs are smaller than average. The second chart shows each job's margin less its estimated margin: 63% of jobs came in below their estimate, by a median of 9 points, and the red bars are the 13% more than 20 points below. The gap includes the price movement between quote and job as well as the jobs taking more than their estimates; Section 2 separates the two. Each bar is labeled with its number of jobs.

2025 Job Margin Distribution
2025 Actual vs. Estimated Job Margin

Repeat parts earn more than new quoted work and miss their estimates by more. Repeat parts earn 27.6% on revenue and new work 22.6%; each loses money on 7% and 8% of its jobs. Against their estimates, repeat parts miss by an average of 7.1 points and new work by 2.9. A repeat part's estimate comes from its original quote, so its gap carries every movement in material, rates and standards since then; a new part's estimate is weeks old. The panels in each chart share a scale.

2025 Job Margin, by Job Type
2025 Actual vs. Estimated Job Margin, by Job Type

Job size separates margin more sharply than job type. Lots under 25 pieces average 13.6% a job and lose money on 19% of them; lots of 25 to 100 pieces average 22.4% and lose money on 6%, and lots over 100 pieces average 24.2% and lose money on 3%. The small lots also miss their estimates by the most, an average of 11.6 points against 4.7 and 2.9. Setup is why a small lot is thin to begin with: it costs the same whatever the lot, so it is 38% of a small lot's estimated cost against 9% for lots over 100, and small lots are estimated at 25.3% against 27.1%.

Section 2

Actual Cost against Estimate, by Element

The estimates on the 2025 jobs promised 28.8% on the year's revenue. Re-costed at the prices of each job's own day (its hours at the job's own pool rate, its material at the job's issue price) they come to 26.9%, and the jobs earned 25.4%. The first 1.9 points are what material prices and labor rates moved between quote and job, a pricing question taken up in Section 5. The other 1.5 points are the jobs taking more than their estimates: actual cost of $41.85M against a re-costed estimate of $41.00M, $852K over (96% of the cost measured). That net figure is $3.49M over estimate on some jobs and elements less $2.63M under on others.

The chart ranks the elements by what ran over. Each bar is the cost over estimate on the jobs where the element ran over; the bar below the axis is what the same element came in under on the other jobs, and the diamond is the net. Outside processing is drawn in three parts: PO invoices over the estimate, PO invoices on jobs whose estimate carries no outside processing because no quote line was found for them, and the ledger residual allocated to jobs, hatched, which no estimate carries. Below the axis, the hatched part is the estimate on jobs with no purchase order tied to them: it is the counterpart of the allocation and not an underrun. The table gives each part its own row.

Run hours ran $1.70M over on 2,981 jobs and $1.49M under on the rest, a median of 1.08× the estimate. The routing standard is time in cycle, while a job's run hours also carry the alarms and in-operation idle the machines record, 23.9% of machine time (96% of the cost measured). Standards set above the measured cycle (1,001 operations more than 15% above it) absorb that on some parts, which is the under side. Standards below the measured cycle cost $315K on 1,203 jobs (96% of the cost measured), the two older vertical mills $126K on the 643 jobs the schedule put on them (96% of the cost measured), and the hard alloys $194K: titanium and Inconel jobs ran 1.11× their estimated run hours against 1.04× for the other materials in the same two families (99% of the cost measured).

Outside processing has three parts, visible going forward because every purchase order now carries a job number. The first is the age of the quote the estimate comes from: PO invoices run 1.05× the estimate where the part was quoted within six months of the job and 1.22× where it was quoted more than three years before, which is vendor drift on every service. The second is the vendors' minimum charges on small lots: 748 of the year's 3,691 PO lines were invoiced at a minimum, $39K more than the per-piece price times the pieces (95% of the cost measured), and jobs with a line at a minimum run 1.75× their estimate against 1.07× for the rest. The third is not an overrun at all. $497K of 2025 outside-processing cost was on purchase orders with no job number that could not be tied to a job afterwards, and is spread over the month's jobs so the ledger reconciles; $467K of it lands on jobs that are over estimate and is the hatched bar. Its other side is the 387 jobs whose estimate carries outside processing and which have no purchase order tied to them, $372K of estimate with nothing set against it. A further $220K sits on 203 jobs with no quote line, whose estimate carries no outside processing to compare with. On the 3,181 jobs that have both an estimate and a purchase order, invoices came to 1.05× the estimates in total, $176K over.

Setup hours run near or under the standard on parts the shop knows and over where something is new: the median job took 0.84× its estimated setup on a part run within the year, 1.59× on the first run after a revision, and on the mill-turn and 5-axis cells a new part or one not run in a year takes 1.62× the routing standard against 1.02× for a part the cell ran within the year. A job stopped for another carries a second setup when it resumes: the record shows one on 62 jobs, $13K (97% of the cost measured).

Scrap and rework are not in the estimate, so all $124K of it is over, on 573 jobs (96% of the cost measured). The figure is a floor: before the labor codes most rework was posted as run time (870 events the audit found), and those hours sit in the run-hours bar.

Material is flat once it is issued at actual and compared at the job's issue price: $107K over and $123K under.

Section 3

What the Blended Rate Hid

The ERP costed every labor hour at one blended shop rate, $178 in 2025 and $185 in 2026. The work-center pools, as set in May 2026, run from $102 an hour at deburr to $277 at the 5-axis cell. Costed at the pools, the families that run on the manual and secondary cells gain (Fixtures and tooling +6.6 points, Weldments and assemblies +6.5) and the families that run on the expensive cells lose (Aerospace brackets -7.4, Turbine components -2.9). Aerospace brackets is the shop's best family at the blended rate and number 8 of 11 at the pools. The blended rate left $902K of cost out of the 2 families it underpriced, $1.15M at the markup price, and overstated the cost of the other 9 by $1.41M (96% of the cost measured). This is what the "labor rate" movements in the repricing queue are.

Section 4

Jobs Caught in Progress

The job cost screen flags a job while it is open: at the first operation where its labor hours to date exceed the estimate to date by more than 15% and by at least two hours, or at the first material issue where material exceeds the estimate by more than 15% and $150. The flag is replayed here over the 4,355 jobs completed from the 2025 releases, to show what the shop could have known and when.

The Flag Replayed over the 2025 Jobs

1,064 jobs would have been flagged, 1,014 of them with operations still to run and 494 with operations left and 3 or more days before the job shipped (96% of the cost measured). Those 494 jobs ran $1.06M over their estimates, and $308K of it (29%) came after the flag: on operations that started after it, and on material issued and outside processing received after it. That is the part a warning could have changed.

A flag allows four things, none of them automatic. Check the routing standard and the program before the next operation runs. Move the remaining operations to another machine. Call the customer about the quantity, the delivery or a change order. Or finish the job knowing what it will cost.

The Flag at Three Thresholds

10%1,25260665 (5%)$320K$1.16M28%
15%1,06449440 (4%)$308K$1.06M29%

At 10% the flag fires on more jobs and more of them recover on their own by close; at 20% it fires later and less of the overrun is still ahead of it. 15% keeps most of the overrun that comes after the flag with fewer flags to work.

Section 5

Repricing

Exposure. At today's material prices, pool rates and measured standards, 262 of the 1,600 repeat parts (16%) have a standing price below current cost plus the shop's standard 28% markup (the markup price), carrying 11% of repeat revenue. The gap is modest on most of them: a median of 5.1%, with nine in ten under 17%; 4 sit below cost outright. At current volume the exposure is $236K a year, and the own-product line adds $355K: together 1.1% of 2025 revenue. The gap is what the annual across-the-board letters (3.0% to 3.5% a year) missed on the parts whose inputs moved most: since the last quote, current cost rose a median 22% on the parts below the markup price against 1% on the rest, while the letters raised the standing prices of those parts a median 9%.

What is defensible. In the shop's experience, as the owner and the controller described it, a routine annual increase of 3 to 5% is accepted without discussion. A larger increase can land selectively, part by part, when the cost driver is documented, and most often that driver is material passed through at what it now costs. Beyond that the relationship risk is real, and the owner decides.

Decisions. The controller and the owner decided every part below the markup price in weeks 7 to 9 on that basis: a gap within the routine range was repriced; a larger gap was repriced where material or outside processing drove it and the movement could be shown part by part, and held otherwise with the reason recorded; a large gap on a small part was exited, and on the 17 largest programs the increase was taken in two steps, half now and the balance at the blanket renewal.

Pricing the Release

A standing price is set for a quoted lot, and a blanket release is whatever the customer calls off. In 2025, 72 of the 2,503 repeat-part releases (2.9%) were below half the lot the price was quoted at. The setup is the same whatever the release, so those jobs carried it over fewer pieces than the price assumed: they earned 16.0% against 27.8% on the other repeat releases, and 39% of them lost money. Charging the part of the estimated setup the price did not cover, (1 less released over quoted) times the estimated setup hours at the pool rate, would have added $22K to those releases and taken them to 20.5% (96% of the cost measured). The action is a setup line on any release below half the quoted lot, or a minimum lot charge on the standing price.

Section 6

The Jobs That Lost Money

322 jobs lost money in 2025, $224,228 in total (95% of the cost measured). Set against their estimates, the losses are mostly not a pricing story: only 32 of the 322 were estimated to lose money before they started. The other 290 were estimated to make money, a median estimated margin of 22%, and lost it in the job; they carry 74% of the loss. Each job carries the driver the reporting layer assigns by rule, the same rules the Job Variance report applies to every job (appendix), and the action the driver maps to: correct the routing standard, correct the quote, bill the change order, reprice the part, fix the process, or accept it as a one-off. This is the list the owner and estimator work from, and it matches what they see in the ERP.

Section 7

Same Part, Different Outcomes

For the 304 repeat parts with three or more jobs in 2025, the gap between each part's best and worst job has a median of 14 points; on 34% of them it is 20 points or more. Same part, same customer, same standing price, different outcome.

Spread of Job Margin within Each Repeat Part, 2025

Lot size. P-10733 (Swiss turned components, Hill-Thompson) ran 4 jobs in 2025 with a 51-point spread. The standing price was set for the usual lot of 122 pieces. The worst job was a release of 51, 0.42× of it, and the setup is the same whatever the lot: at 51 pieces the estimated setup is 69% of the price against 30% to 33% on the other jobs. The job's own current-cost estimate showed −16.2% before it started, and it earned −23.9% against 26.9% on the best job. Its setup ran 0.94× the estimate and its run hours 1.27×, inside the range of the part's other jobs (1.22× to 1.54×); run hours run over on every job of the part, which is its routing standard and not this release.

Material here is against the estimate as carried, at the prices of the quote, so the 2025 column includes what the price moved; Section 2 re-costs it at the job's issue price. Outside processing is PO invoices over the estimate in both columns, without the ledger residual allocated to 2025 jobs.

Material moved to 1.00 and its spread closed because the estimate now carries the price of the day and not the spreadsheet's price list. Outside processing moved to 1.01 from 1.10 because the quoting module carries the vendors' current prices and minimums. Run hours narrowed, from 0.96 to 1.25 (0.29 wide) to 1.02 to 1.23 (0.21 wide), because repeat parts are now estimated on the measured cycle; and the median rose, from 1.08 to 1.11. Both follow from the refresh. Most refreshed standards had sat above the measured cycle (1,001 operations more than 15% above it against 509 more than 15% below), so the refresh took out a cushion; and the measured cycle is time in cycle, with none of the stoppages a job's run hours carry, 23.9% of machine time. That is the case for a stoppage allowance in the standard. Setup hours have not moved yet (a median of 0.83 against 0.86): 37% of the engagement-period repeat jobs were estimated before their part's refreshed standard took effect, and new and infrequent parts still run over. Labor and burden tightened further because the estimate and the actual now use the same pool rate.

By estimator, the gap between the estimated margin and the margin runs 1.6 to 2.2 points, about the same for all three: the shortfall is in what the estimates carry, not in who writes them. By quote year, the margin on new work has not improved on its own, from 24.3% on work quoted in 2023 to 19.4% on work quoted in 2026; that is what the feedback is for.

Appendix

Method, Definitions and Detail

Job cost. Material at the issued price, corrected to the part's need where the audit found another job's bar or none; labor as hours at the work center's pool rate (labor rate × attended ratio + burden); outside processing at the invoiced price, with lines that could not be tied to a job allocated over the month's jobs; scrap at the job's material cost. CNC hours come from the machine-monitoring feed on every monitored cell, not from the clock record.

Measured share. The share of a job's cost resting on a transaction (a machine interval assigned to the job, a clock record, a scan, an issue, a purchase order) and not on the routing standard, an allocated ledger residual or a record flagged unrepairable. Stated beside every dollar figure as the coverage of the jobs behind it.

Margin. Margin is gross margin: price less the job's cost (material, labor and burden at the work center's pool rate, outside processing and scrapped material), as a share of price. Estimated margin is the same measure on the job's estimate, and a job loses money when its margin is below zero. The shop prices as a markup on cost: its standard 28% markup prices a job at cost × 1.28, a margin of 0.28 ÷ 1.28 = 21.9%.

Actual against estimate. Each job's actual cost less its estimate, with the estimate re-costed at the prices of the job's own day: its hours at the job's pool rate, its material at the job's issue price. The difference splits exactly into the elements: material, setup hours, run hours, outside processing, and scrap and rework, which the estimate does not carry. The outside-processing estimate is the quote line's figure and is not re-costed. A job with no quote line is estimated from the routing standard at the shop rate with material at the month's price, and carries no outside processing in its estimate.

Outside-processing minimum excess. On a PO line invoiced at the vendor's minimum charge, the invoice less the per-piece price times the pieces.

Blended-rate margin. The job costed with every labor hour at the blended shop rate of its year; the pool-rate margin is this report's standard margin. Both are on the same 2025 jobs. The dollars at the markup price are the cost difference times 1.28.

In-progress flag. A job is flagged at the first operation where its labor hours to date exceed the estimate to date by more than 15% and by at least two hours, or at the first material issue if material exceeds the estimate by more than 15% and $150. An operation is a cell on the routing, in routing order. The estimate to date is the routing standard for each operation, scaled so the operations sum to the job's estimated hours. A flag is actionable when it fires before the last operation and 3 or more days before the job ships.

Overrun after the flag. On a job flagged while open: the actual less the estimate on every operation that started after the flag, plus the material and outside-processing variance in proportion to the dollars issued or received after the flag date, net of what came in under estimate there.

Recovered by close. A flagged job whose final cost came in at or under its re-costed estimate.

Release setup charge. On a repeat-part release below half its quoted lot: (1 less released over quoted) × the job's estimated setup hours × the pool rate. The quoted lot is read from the part's quote on file. Own products and new work are excluded.

Revision work. Section 8 states the revision work not billed as the shortfall-by-cause mart sizes it: on a job with a revision after release and no change-order line, the setup and run hours beyond the shop's median labor ratio, at the job's rate. A second measure, the account's hours beyond the rest of the book's ratio of actual to estimated hours, gives $207K for Mendoza-Davis; it is lower because it nets the account's jobs that ran under against those that ran over.

Drivers. Section 6 assigns each job the driver the reporting layer's rules give it, the same rules the Job Variance report shows in the ERP: routing standard (run hours over 1.15× the estimate, and the part's other jobs in the trailing twelve months over too); new or infrequent part setup (setup over 1.30× on a part new to the shop or not run in the past 12 months); unbilled revision work (labor over estimate, a revision change after release and no change order billed, at any customer); vendor rate (outside processing over 1.10× the estimate); scrap and rework (over 5% of estimated cost); material (over the estimate by more than 10%); priced below estimated cost (the job's own estimate showed a loss, sized as that estimated loss). Where several fire, the largest dollar variance is the driver; where none fires, or the largest carries under 40% of the job's overrun, the job is not attributable.
